title: Opening worship and welcome
paragraphs: Yes, Lord. Thank You, Lord. Hallelujah! Hallelujah! Hallelujah!
Peace be with you all in the mighty, glorious, holy, and awesome name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I believe that you will receive a blessing this morning.
I welcome everyone who has come into the house of the Lord. Let us give the Lord a mighty round of applause as we take our seats and glorify His holy name.

This is a blessed morning, and the subject we are going to study from the Word of God is a little different. You may have noticed that I have some papers in my hand. Today I want to introduce a subject that touches the everyday lives of many people.
You can see the title on the screen behind me: “Loans, Interest & Mortgages: Sin or Misunderstanding?”

Today we will examine borrowing, lending, interest, and pledging possessions as security. We want to understand what the Bible teaches and where our understanding may have been shaped by assumptions or misunderstandings.

Here is the central truth I want us to carry throughout this message: God calls us to honesty when we borrow, mercy when we lend, and justice in every financial agreement. Borrowing and pledging property are not automatically sins. Exploitation, deception, and cruelty are never made righteous by a signed agreement.

The difficult question is how the Bible's teaching about interest applies to different situations. We will take that question seriously. We must neither weaken God's commands nor make Scripture say more than it says.

title: Reading Scripture carefully
paragraphs: Before we begin, let us make an important commitment. We will read each passage in its context. A command given to Israel, a prophetic rebuke, a wisdom saying, and a parable of Jesus each require careful attention. They all belong to God's Word, but they do not all function in exactly the same way.
When I explain a passage in simple English, I am giving its meaning rather than quoting a particular Bible translation word for word. Keep your Bible open so that you can read the passage itself.

We will also distinguish what Scripture states directly from how we apply its principles today. Modern banks and mortgages do not appear in the Bible in their present form. That does not leave them outside God's concern. It means we must apply His teaching with care.

title: Questions we need to ask
paragraphs: Is borrowing money a sin? Is lending money to someone a sin? What about borrowing and refusing to repay? What does God say about the responsibilities of the borrower and the lender?

Does the Bible permit interest on a loan? What about money deposited in a bank? Is receiving interest sinful? What about paying it? Can a Christian take out a loan to buy a house or a car, or to start a business?
If interest is forbidden, why do certain biblical passages discuss it differently? Why did Jesus mention interest in His parables?

What about pledging land, a house, jewellery, or property documents as security for a debt? If someone receives the use of farmland as security for a loan and takes its crops or income, how should we understand that arrangement?
Why does the Bible contain instructions about pledges? Is our religious understanding of these matters correct, or have we misunderstood some things?

These questions circulate throughout our society. They are in people's minds, and they affect our homes and livelihoods. We must examine them in the light of Scripture, paying attention to their setting and to the examples God has given us.
Keep your Bible open. We will learn step by step.

title: Why this subject concerns all of us
paragraphs: At some point, most of us have needed help. Is there anyone here who has never borrowed anything? Borrowing is not always limited to money.

Some people buy things in instalments. Others have pledged their jewellery, their homes, or other possessions to meet urgent needs. Some families live in a house under a financial arrangement intended to reduce their rent. Others struggle with the payments on their own home.
These are real social and financial concerns. They affect real families.

But I want to encourage you: we have come together to learn from the Bible. Here at The Church of Pentecost, our foundation must be the Word of God. We must examine our traditions and assumptions in its light. Our eyes are on God's true, living, incomparable, and enduring Word.
How many of you believe that the teaching of Scripture is true? Stay with me. The beauty of the Bible is that it speaks to the practical concerns of human life as well as to our spiritual needs.

Scripture reminds us that there will be poor people among us. Even someone who would not ordinarily describe himself as poor may experience a time of need. There may be school fees to pay, household bills, rent, travel costs, a wedding, repairs, or the construction of a home. Unexpected visitors or circumstances may also create expenses.
So the question is not merely theoretical. What does God require of us when someone needs to borrow? What does He require when we ourselves are the borrowers?

title: A generous heart toward those in need
paragraphs: Let us begin with Deuteronomy 15:7–8. God instructed His people that, if a poor brother lived among them in the land He was giving them, they were not to harden their hearts or close their hands against him. They were to open their hands and lend him enough to meet his need.
Notice the heart of this instruction. Do not harden your heart. Do not close your hand.
How many believers are here today? How many believe in the Lord Jesus Christ? This is a simple teaching, but it reaches into our pockets and touches our cheque books!
When your brother is in need, God does not want your heart to become hard. He calls you to respond with generosity.
This word is for you, and it is for me. In our families and among our relatives, there are people who sometimes need help. The question is how we respond when they come to us.
Someone may be thinking, “Pastor, people have come to me before. I lent them money, and they never paid me back. After lending, I had to keep chasing them.”
That is a real concern. So let us look at what Scripture says to the person who borrows.

title: The responsibility to repay
paragraphs: Psalm 37:21 describes the wicked person as one who borrows and does not repay, while the righteous person is generous and gives.
The Bible speaks to both sides of the relationship. It calls the lender to mercy and generosity, and it calls the borrower to honesty.

If you borrow, do not treat someone else's kindness as an opportunity to deceive them. Do not make a promise that you have no intention of keeping. Do not borrow from your brother and then deny your responsibility.

Proverbs 22:7 tells us that the rich rule over the poor and that the borrower is servant to the lender. Debt creates an obligation. It can limit a person's freedom and place pressure upon a household.
This is why borrowing must be approached responsibly. When you receive a loan, make every effort to repay it as agreed. Be truthful about your circumstances.
At the same time, Scripture also recognises the plight of people who genuinely cannot pay. We must not forget the command to show mercy while we speak about the responsibility to repay.
Psalm 112:5 describes the good person as generous in lending and just in conducting his affairs. Generosity and justice belong together. Lending should be an act of help, carried out fairly.

title: The year of release in Israel
paragraphs: Under the law given to Israel, there was a year of release. Deuteronomy 15:1–2 instructed God's people to release debts at the end of every seven years. A creditor was not to continue demanding payment from his fellow Israelite when the Lord's release had been proclaimed.

This was a remarkable expression of mercy within Israel's covenant life. Debt was not to become an endless burden from which a poor family could never escape. This was the community’s appointed seventh-year release, not simply a separate seven-year countdown beginning whenever each loan was made. It is not a promise that modern bank debts automatically expire every seven years.
But God also knew the human heart. In Deuteronomy 15:9, He warned His people not to refuse help because the year of release was approaching.
Imagine someone saying, “The year of release is almost here. If I lend now, I may never get my money back. So I will give him nothing.”
God warned against that attitude. The approaching year of release was not an excuse for closing one's hand against a needy brother.
Are you following me? This was part of the law given to Israel. It shows us how seriously God regarded both human need and the danger of a hardened heart.
Borrowing itself is not automatically a sin. A person may face circumstances in which help is necessary. But dishonesty about a debt is a serious matter.

Psalm 37 also speaks of the righteous person's generosity and God's care for the righteous and their children. My prayer is that we will grow into people who can help others. If we need to borrow, let us do so honestly. If we can lend, let us do so mercifully.

title: What Jesus teaches about lending
paragraphs: Now let us turn to Luke 6:32–36.

Jesus asks what credit there is in loving only those who love us, or doing good only to those who do good to us. Even sinners do that. He then speaks about lending only to those from whom we expect repayment.
We understand this very well. Before lending, we may ask, “Does this person earn enough? Does he have the means to repay? Where will he get the money?”
Sometimes a person asks for more than his income seems able to support, and immediately we say, “How will he ever pay it back?”

But Jesus takes us beyond a relationship governed only by the possibility of receiving something in return. He tells us to love our enemies, do good, and lend without expecting anything back. He speaks of a great reward and of being children of the Most High, who is kind even to the ungrateful and the wicked.
Then He says that we are to be merciful as our Father is merciful.

This calls for a change in our thinking. Can we help someone without allowing the possibility of repayment to control our compassion? Can we give help without allowing disappointment to turn into hatred?

When we show mercy, we reflect the character of our Father. Our generosity is not a price with which we purchase a place in God's family; it expresses the mercy of the Father whose children we are called to be.
Think about the greatness of the God we serve. Heaven is His throne, and the earth is His footstool. Everything belongs to Him. Why should we imagine that showing mercy will place us beyond His care?

It is easy to applaud this teaching. It is harder to put it into practice! If I say, “Go home and consider whom you need to forgive,” suddenly the matter becomes personal. Yet this is where the Word of God meets our lives.

title: A widow threatened by debt
paragraphs: In 2 Kings 4:1–7, we read about a widow whose husband had served the Lord. He had died, and a creditor was coming to take her two sons as servants because of the debt.
She came to Elisha in distress. Her husband was gone, the debt remained, and now her children were in danger of being taken away.

Debt can bring terrible pressure into a home. I remember witnessing an incident when I was a student. A lender came to a house near where I lived and demanded his money. The borrower kept asking him to be patient, but he continued insisting on payment. Eventually he entered the house to press his demand.
I remember how distressing that situation was. Lending can become an occasion for humiliation when mercy disappears.

We see other painful examples in our society. In Punjab, some families have become bound to years of labour because of debts. Parents borrow, children grow up under the burden, and another generation remains trapped.

Think of families working at brick kilns. Think of children getting up early to make bricks. Think of workers who care for livestock, clean, and perform exhausting tasks while remaining dependent on the people to whom they owe money.
Behind these situations are families, children, and human dignity. We must not speak about debt as though it were only a number on a page.

The widow told Elisha that she had only a little oil. He instructed her to gather empty vessels. God provided through the multiplication of that oil, and she was told to sell it, pay her debt, and live with her sons on what remained.
The provision addressed her debt and protected her children. What a powerful testimony of God's care for a desperate household!

title: Forgiveness and the response of love
paragraphs: In Luke 7:41–43, Jesus speaks of two people who owed money to a creditor. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other owed fifty. Neither could repay, and the creditor forgave them both.
Jesus asked which of them would love him more. The answer was the one whose greater debt had been forgiven.
Forgiveness awakens gratitude. Mercy changes relationships.

Matthew 18:23–35 describes a servant whose enormous debt is forgiven by a king. The servant then refuses mercy to a fellow servant who owes him far less and has him imprisoned. The king condemns this cruelty. The central challenge is that those who receive mercy must show mercy. The parable is not a general instruction that every financial contract must be cancelled immediately; it confronts the unforgiving heart.

As a servant of God, I want to say this plainly: many people are trapped in debt upon debt. Their lives have become miserable under the pressure. As Christians, we must take seriously the words of Jesus about compassion, generosity, and forgiveness.

title: Understanding the words
paragraphs: A loan is something entrusted to another person with an obligation to return it or its agreed equivalent. The principal is the original amount borrowed. Interest is an additional charge connected with the loan. A pledge is an asset given or committed as security. A modern mortgage is a loan secured against property; its precise terms depend on the agreement and the applicable law.

These distinctions matter. Borrowing, charging interest, and taking security are related, but they are not identical actions. A loan may be interest free and still involve security. A loan may charge interest without requiring a pledged possession.

The Hebrew word neshek means interest on a debt. Tarbit refers to an increase or an amount added to the principal. The Greek word tokos is used for interest in Matthew 25:27 and Luke 19:23. These words help us understand what the text is discussing; they do not, by themselves, settle the morality of every modern financial product.

The Urdu words sood and byaaj often overlap in ordinary use. We should not assume that one means a permitted charge and the other a forbidden charge simply because both appear in a translation. We must examine the original terms, the sentence, and the circumstances being addressed.

title: Interest and the burden of borrowing
paragraphs: Let us now consider interest.
In ordinary financial life, borrowing is often connected with interest. Whether you live in Pakistan, Canada, or elsewhere, you will encounter loans, credit cards, and repayment agreements.

If a credit card balance is not paid according to its terms, interest may be charged. If someone cannot keep up with mortgage payments, the home may be at risk. Similar pressures arise with vehicles and goods bought in instalments.

I recently heard about someone with a beautiful home who fell behind on the payments and lost possession of it. We also know situations in which sellers come to recover household goods because the instalments have not been paid.
These matters cause real fear and distress. So we must listen carefully to what God says about how we treat people who need financial help.

title: Do not profit from your brother's distress
paragraphs: Exodus 22:25 addresses lending to the poor among God's people. It tells the lender not to act as a harsh creditor and not to charge interest in that situation.
I am speaking to believers, to people who receive the Bible as the Word of God and seek to follow the teaching of Jesus Christ. We cannot separate our financial behaviour from our faith.

Leviticus 25:35–37 speaks of a brother who becomes poor and cannot support himself. God's people are instructed to help him so that he can continue to live among them. They are not to take interest or profit from him, but to fear God. The passage speaks about money and also about food.

Notice the setting: a brother has become poor, his position is weak, and he needs help to survive. God calls His people to support him. His distress must not become our opportunity to enrich ourselves.
If you provide money, food, or other necessities to someone in that condition, remember the purpose of your help. You are helping him live. Do not turn that help into a burden that crushes him.
Someone may say, “Pastor, one day you preach about offerings, another day about lending, and another day about helping the poor!”

But money touches so much of everyday life. Our children need education. Our families need food and shelter. We must meet ordinary expenses. It is therefore right that we allow God's Word to examine how we earn, lend, spend, and give.

title: Righteousness in our financial dealings
paragraphs: Psalm 15:5 includes refusing to lend at interest and refusing to accept a bribe against the innocent in its description of the righteous life.
Ezekiel 18:8 describes a righteous person who does not lend at interest or take an increase, who withdraws his hand from wrongdoing, and who judges fairly between people.

Ezekiel 18:13 speaks severely about the person who charges interest and takes an increase as part of a life of wrongdoing. Ezekiel 22:12 also condemns interest, unjust gain, and the oppression of one's neighbours.
These are serious passages. We must not brush them aside merely because a practice is common or profitable.

The challenge I am placing before believers is this: do not use someone else's need as a way to exploit them. Do not call a practice righteous simply because you have given it a respectable name. Examine what it actually does to your neighbour.
Does it help someone stand again, or does it keep that person under pressure? Is it conducted with justice, or does it humiliate and consume a family?
God is concerned about what happens in our neighbourhoods, in our homes, and in our dealings with one another.

title: Why Deuteronomy mentions an exception
paragraphs: Now let us face a question from our introduction. If the Bible condemns interest in these passages, why does it also contain permission to charge it?

Deuteronomy 23:19–20 forbids an Israelite from charging interest to a fellow Israelite on money, food, or anything lent at interest. It then permits charging interest to a foreigner. The distinction is there in the text; we must not hide it.

Notice also that the wording about a fellow Israelite is broader than a statement only against exceptionally high rates. We should not rewrite the verse as though it merely said, “Do not charge too much.” At the same time, its stated exception prevents us from saying that the law prohibited every interest payment in every relationship without distinction.

This instruction belonged to Israel's covenant and community life. It does not give us permission to deceive or mistreat people outside our church, nationality, or religion. Jesus calls us to love even our enemies. A Christian cannot use the word “foreigner” as an excuse to abandon mercy.

This is why Christians differ over how these laws apply today. Some understand the biblical prohibitions very broadly. Others distinguish lending to relieve poverty from fair commercial lending and modern banking. Our study must acknowledge that difference while holding firmly to the clear commands against oppression and dishonesty.

title: Why Jesus mentioned interest in His parables
paragraphs: In Matthew 25:14–30, a master entrusts property to his servants. Two put what they receive to work, while another buries his master's money. In verse 27, the master says that depositing the money with bankers would at least have produced interest. Luke 19:23 includes a similar statement in the parable of the minas.

What is Jesus teaching through these stories? He calls His hearers to faithfulness and accountability with what has been entrusted to them. The servant's inactivity exposes his failure to act faithfully.

The mention of interest is part of the story's argument. It is not a detailed instruction approving every loan, every interest rate, or every method of collection. Nor should we pretend that the reference is absent because it makes our interpretation more difficult.
Read the parables together with the laws protecting the poor and the prophets' condemnation of exploitation. One verse from a parable cannot carry the whole weight of Christian financial ethics.

title: Savings accounts and borrowing for a home or business
paragraphs: Someone asks, “Pastor, may a Christian receive interest from a savings account?” Another asks, “May I borrow to buy a home, a vehicle, or equipment for a business?”

The Bible does not name these modern products and give a separate ruling on each one. The fact that an arrangement involves a bank does not automatically make it righteous; neither does the mere presence of a modern banking term establish that it is sinful.

Christians who accept the distinction between prohibited exploitative lending and fair commercial finance may consider an ordinary savings account or a responsibly undertaken mortgage permissible. Christians who hold a stricter interpretation may refrain. We should explain our reasons from Scripture and avoid condemning a person's faith merely because their bank account or housing arrangement differs from ours.

For any proposed agreement, examine the actual terms. Is there deception? Is a vulnerable person being taken advantage of? Are the charges clear? Are promises being made honestly? Does the arrangement place a foreseeable, unmanageable burden on the household? These are practical questions arising from honesty, justice, and responsible stewardship.

Receiving a bank's approval is not the same as receiving God's instruction to borrow. Nor does declining a loan demonstrate a lack of faith. Pray, understand the agreement, and seek competent help where its terms are unclear.

Do not borrow merely to impress others. Do not hide debt from the people who share responsibility for the household. And do not tell someone in financial distress that taking another loan is proof that they trust God.
The question is larger than, “Can I obtain this money?” We must also ask, “Can I fulfil this obligation honestly, and does this arrangement honour God and treat people fairly?”

title: Parents and children are accountable to God
paragraphs: Ezekiel 18 begins with a proverb about parents eating sour grapes and their children's teeth being set on edge.

People were using this saying to describe the relationship between the conduct of one generation and the experience of another. But God confronts the idea that a child must bear the moral guilt of a parent's sin.
The chapter teaches that the person who sins is accountable for that sin. Ezekiel 18:20 states this principle plainly.

Suppose a father acts unjustly. Suppose the income brought into a household comes through exploitation. His children may experience the effects of that household's choices, but that does not mean that God treats an innocent child as personally guilty of the father's conduct.

Ezekiel describes a son who sees his father's wrongdoing and does not follow it. He refuses oppression, obeys God's commands, and does not continue the unjust practices of the previous generation. That son is not condemned for his father's sin.
Young people, you do not have to repeat every practice you have seen at home. When you begin earning, when you enter business, and when you make financial decisions, you can choose obedience to God.

Parents, this also challenges us. What example are we setting? What kind of livelihood are we placing before our children? Are we teaching them mercy and justice, or teaching them to squeeze profit out of other people's distress?
Let us ask God to make our homes places of honest work and righteous dealings.

title: A community called to account
paragraphs: Nehemiah 5:1–13 describes a crisis among God's people. Families needed food. Some had pledged fields, vineyards, and houses. Others had borrowed to pay taxes. Their children were suffering, and the people cried out.
Nehemiah confronted the exploitation taking place among brothers. This was not merely an accounting problem. It was a matter of justice within the community of God's people.
We should hear that challenge today. We must not worship together while ignoring the suffering that our own financial practices may cause.

Isaiah 24:2 also places lenders and borrowers alike within the reach of God's judgment. No financial position puts us beyond accountability to Him. The verse describes the breadth of judgment across social positions; it does not, by itself, declare every act of borrowing or lending sinful.
Whether we lend or borrow, we must examine our lives before the Lord. Let the lender practise mercy and fairness. Let the borrower practise honesty and responsibility.

title: Pledges and mortgages under the care of God
paragraphs: Let us now turn to the third part of our subject: pledging possessions and securing a debt. In Urdu, we commonly speak of girvi or rehn. The pledged item provides security for an obligation. Yet the presence of security does not give a lender unlimited authority over the borrower's life.

The Bible regulates pledges. That means a pledge is not treated as inherently forbidden in every circumstance. But the regulations place important limits on what may be taken and how the borrower must be treated.
In Exodus 22:26–27, a neighbour's cloak taken as a pledge is to be returned before nightfall. God draws attention to the person's need for covering and promises to hear the cry of the distressed.

Think about that picture. The creditor is thinking about security. God also asks us to think about the person trying to sleep through the night. A financial claim does not erase a neighbour's humanity.

Deuteronomy 24:6 protects the millstones used in preparing food. The household's means of sustenance must not be taken as security. The moral principle is profound: do not destroy the means by which a struggling family lives.

Deuteronomy 24:10–13 also sets limits on the creditor's conduct. The lender must wait outside while the borrower brings out the pledge. Poverty does not cancel a person's dignity or the boundaries of their home.

Deuteronomy 24:17 gives particular protection to the widow and requires justice for the foreigner and the fatherless. These instructions reveal God's concern for those least able to defend themselves.

Taken together, these passages challenge us to examine the item pledged, the borrower's essential needs, and the lender's conduct. A signature cannot turn humiliation or oppression into an act of righteousness.

title: Other biblical examples of security and abuse
paragraphs: Genesis 38:17–20 records Judah leaving his seal, cord, and staff with Tamar as a pledge for something he promised to send. This is an example of a pledge securing a promise, rather than an ordinary money loan. Its morally troubled setting must not be treated as an approved model for our conduct. It helps explain the function of a pledge; it does not endorse everything in the story.

Job 24:2–9 describes abuses against vulnerable people. Among them are the seizure of an orphan's donkey and the taking of a widow's ox as a pledge. These images expose what happens when powerful people deprive the weak of the resources on which they depend.

Proverbs 22:26–27 warns about guaranteeing another person's debt when you cannot meet the obligation. It pictures even a person's bed being taken away. This is a warning to take promises seriously. Compassion should not lead us to make commitments we do not understand or cannot fulfil.

We have already seen in Nehemiah 5 how pledged fields, vineyards, and houses became part of a community crisis. Nehemiah did not tell the suffering families merely to remain quiet. He confronted the powerful and called for concrete change.
We too must care about what an agreement does to a family. Are they being helped toward stability, or drawn into dependence from which they cannot escape?

title: A farmer who pledges his land
paragraphs: Consider the example in our study. A farmer pledges five acres of land against a loan of one million Pakistani rupees. The lender receives the crops produced by the land and later also demands the full original one million rupees.

Before declaring the arrangement acceptable, we must ask what is actually happening. Is the crop income credited against the debt? Who pays the costs of cultivation? Who bears the risk if the harvest fails? Can the farmer recover the land when the agreed obligation is discharged?

If the lender takes the net produce solely because the money was lent, while the entire principal remains payable, the produce is an additional economic benefit attached to the loan. Calling it a “gift” or “use of the land” does not make that benefit disappear. It deserves the same moral scrutiny as other charges for borrowing.

But we should not automatically classify every crop-sharing arrangement as interest. A genuine lease, a partnership sharing costs and risks, or an arrangement that credits the crop proceeds toward repayment may operate differently. We must examine the substance of the agreement and its fairness.

Here are the questions I want us to remember. Is the farmer's need being relieved or exploited? Is the family losing its means of survival? Are costs, proceeds, and repayment recorded honestly? Is the lender receiving more than the parties fairly agreed? Is the land returned when the obligation has been met?

The same kind of examination applies when a home is occupied in exchange for a large refundable advance. If the advance must be returned in full and free occupancy is the lender's benefit for providing it, the arrangement needs careful examination. The name people use for it does not settle its moral character.
Beloved, the farmer's tears matter to God. The lender's honesty matters to God. The agreement itself matters. We must not use a religious label to conceal an unjust practice.

title: Practising this teaching in our homes and church
paragraphs: To the borrower, I say: be truthful about what you owe. Keep a clear record. If you cannot meet an agreed payment, communicate honestly instead of disappearing. Do not confuse another person's compassion with permission to deceive them.

To the lender, I say: ask what help the person actually needs. Sometimes a gift is more appropriate than a loan. Sometimes patience, a revised arrangement, or forgiveness is the merciful response. Never use threats, shame, or a person's children as instruments of pressure.

To the church, I say: let our teaching be accompanied by practical care. We can listen to struggling families, help them understand their responsibilities, and connect them with trustworthy assistance. Where exploitation has occurred, repentance should include making wrongs right where possible, as Nehemiah's example challenges us to do.

To everyone, I say: do not measure a person's spiritual worth by the size of their income or the absence of debt. The widow in 2 Kings 4 belonged to a household that served God, yet she experienced severe financial distress. Poverty is not proof that God has rejected someone.

We pray confidently for God's provision, but we do not promise that every believer will become wealthy or that every debt will vanish immediately. God also works through honest employment, wise decisions, patient support, and the generosity of His people.

title: Our response to the Word
paragraphs: Beloved, this message calls us to examine our hearts.

Before borrowing, take your responsibility seriously. Before lending, consider mercy and justice. Do not use another person's hardship as an opportunity for oppression. Do not take advantage of someone else's generosity.
Where we have done wrong, let us repent. Where we have hardened our hearts, let us ask God to soften them. Where our financial habits have brought harm, let us turn toward honesty and righteousness.
Above all, let us trust the God who knows our needs. My prayer is that we will not remain crushed beneath debt, but will become people through whom others receive help and blessing.

title: Prayer for provision and freedom from financial burdens
paragraphs: Please lift your hands before the Lord. Wherever you are listening, whether here in the church or online, join us in prayer.
God knows the work of your hands. He knows your employment, your business, your income, and the responsibilities you carry. Bring them before Him now.
Jabez called upon God and asked for His blessing, for his territory to be enlarged, and for God's hand to be with him. Today, let us also bring our lives before the Lord.

Heavenly Father, in the name of Jesus Christ, I bring before You every person listening to this message. I pray for the families standing here and for those joining us from their homes and from other places.
Lord, You have placed these people upon my heart. Together we lift our hands before You. We agree in prayer as brothers and sisters, sons and daughters, asking for Your mercy and provision.
Bless their employment. Bless the work of their hands. Give strength to their bodies, clarity to their minds, and wisdom for their decisions. Open doors for honest work and fruitful businesses.
Lord, increase the resources available to families who are struggling. Where their circumstances have become barren, let there be refreshment. Where they see no way forward, make a way.

Father, I pray for those who are afraid of losing their homes, their vehicles, or the possessions they need for daily life. I pray for those whose properties and jewellery have been pledged and who long to recover them.
Look upon their tears. Hear their cries and their petitions. In the name of Jesus, open doors of help and provision. Lead them out of despair and give them wisdom for each step ahead.
Let everyone listening open their mouth and pray: “Lord, bless me. Lord, bless the work of my hands. Help me to move forward. Let my life become fruitful.”
Father, let Your blessing reach their homes. Let opportunities open before them. Let the earth yield its fruit, and provide from Your good treasure in heaven.
I pray for growth in their work, their businesses, and their resources. You are able to do far more than we can imagine. I ask for abundant provision according to Your wisdom and goodness.
Teach us to use what You give us faithfully. Make us honest, righteous, and merciful people. As You help us, make us ready to help others.
We place our needs, our families, and our future into Your hands. In the mighty name of Jesus Christ, amen.

title: Tithes offerings and partnership in the Gospel
paragraphs: You may take your seats. May the Lord bless you as you bring your tithes and offerings before Him and support His work.
I also want to speak to everyone listening online. If you have been blessed through this ministry, please prayerfully consider supporting the work of the church.
There are many responsibilities before us. We are sharing the Gospel, serving people, and carrying forward the church's projects and social ministry. Your support helps this work continue.

I have also appealed for help with two cameras for our media ministry. At the time of this appeal, we have received two hundred thousand Pakistani rupees toward that need. We are grateful for every gift, but further support is needed to obtain the equipment.

If you would like to partner with us, please use the giving information provided by the church. You can visit our website for the available giving options and contact us for the correct payment details.
Through this digital ministry, the Gospel is reaching people beyond the walls of a church building. Your generosity helps us continue bringing God's Word to listeners around the world.
Thank you for standing with us, for praying with us, and for supporting the work of the Gospel. May God bless you and your household.

title: Scripture guide for further study
paragraphs: Borrowing and lending: Deuteronomy 15:1–11; Psalm 37:21, 25–26; Psalm 112:5; Proverbs 22:7; Luke 6:32–36.
Mercy and forgiveness: 2 Kings 4:1–7; Luke 7:41–43; Matthew 18:23–35.
Interest and justice: Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35–37; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Psalm 15:5; Ezekiel 18:5–20; Ezekiel 22:12; Nehemiah 5:1–13.
Interest in the parables: Matthew 25:14–30, especially verse 27; Luke 19:11–27, especially verse 23.
Pledges and protection of the vulnerable: Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:6, 10–13, 17; Proverbs 22:26–27; Genesis 38:17–20; Job 24:2–9; Nehemiah 5:3–5.
Prayer and accountability: 1 Chronicles 4:9–10; Isaiah 24:1–3. Read each passage within its surrounding chapter.
